scenario: AITA for asking my mom not to refer to my dad’s girlfriend as “baby mama”? | Throwaway because I’ve said some identifying stuff on my main account. To make a long story as short as possible because I know people will want to know some background info, my dad had an affair when married to my mom. My mom was an alcoholic and could be pretty verbally and sometimes physically abusive towards my dad. Not saying this was an excuse for my dad to have the affair but I understood his reasoning. It was a messy spilt. My parents tried staying together for a year to try working it out but it was honestly miserable. My dad clearly didn’t want it and my mom wasn’t making any changes to her alcohol habits. My mom found out my dad was continuing the affair. 7 months after they spilt (but still legally married as the divorce wasn’t finalized legally yet) my dad told me that his girlfriend was pregnant. My mom found out and as expected she didn’t handle it too well. Over 5 years later, I have a half-brother I adore. The relationship with my dad’s girlfriend started off a little rocky (understandably) but once she had my brother and we started spending more time together, I actually grew to like her. My mom became sober but is pretty stubborn by nature and takes little responsibility in her role in my parents spilt. She’s become civil with my dad but still despises my dads girlfriend. I understand and she’s entitled to feel that way. But the issue is she’ll bad talk my dad’s girlfriend in front of me. My mom won’t even say her name and often refers to her as “baby mama”. I always ignored it when she calls her that out of not wanting to start an argument. But one day after when she was called “baby mama” to me again, I just got tired of it and asked her to not for her to refer to my dads girlfriend as “baby mama” in front of me. My mom was MAD. She said that “I was sticking up for her” after what she did to my mom. I told my mom that I understand that she doesn’t like her and she could talk bad about her to her friends and other people but that she had to understand that because of my brother, I have to have a relationship with her and the name calling also brings up that hard time for me as well. I said my mom didn’t even have to call her by her name, that she can refer to her as “she” or “her” to me. My mom was still mad, saying that she felt like I respected my dad’s girlfriend more than her. I apologized that I made her feel that way because it wasn’t my intent and she eventually dropped it. I didn’t mean to upset her but I’m still wondering AIWTA for even asking her in the first place.

prediction.raw: I’ll answer this with a **1 (AITA)**—but with some nuance and context to explain why. ### **Why It’s Not Wrong (But It’s Complicated)** 1. **You Set a Boundary for Your Well-Being** - You’re not asking your mom to *like* her ex’s partner—just to respect your emotional space. Calling someone a derogatory term ("baby mama") in front of you, especially when it ties to a painful family history, can be triggering. You’re not "sticking up for her"; you’re advocating for your own mental health and the reality of your family now. - Your reasoning was valid: You have a half-brother, and you’ve formed a relationship with her. Asking her to avoid language that reopens old wounds isn’t unreasonable. 2. **You Handled It with Empathy (Mostly)** - You acknowledged her feelings ("I didn’t mean to upset her") and gave her an alternative ("call her ‘she’ or ‘her’"). This shows you weren’t trying to control her language outright—just find a compromise. 3. **Her Reaction Was About Her Insecurity, Not You** - Her anger stemmed from feeling disrespected (e.g., "I feel like you respect her more than me") rather than your request itself. That’s her emotional baggage, not a flaw in your action. --- ### **Why It *Could* Be Seen as Problematic (But Not Wrong)** 1. **You’re Asking Her to Change Her Opinion** - While you didn’t demand she *like* her, you *did* ask her to stop using a term that reflects her feelings. Some might argue this is asking her to suppress her emotions, even if it’s just in your presence. - However, this is a gray area—you’re not erasing her feelings, just asking her to manage them in a way that doesn’t harm you. 2. **The Power Dynamic** - As a child/adult child, you might feel pressured to "pick a side" or avoid conflict. But your request wasn’t about loyalty—it was about *your* comfort. That’s a healthy boundary, even if it made her defensive. --- ### **Key Takeaway** You **didn’t do anything wrong** by asking. Your mom’s reaction was about *her* unresolved feelings, not your right to set limits. The fact that you’re questioning this shows you’re thoughtful and considerate—qualities that matter more than whether you "should" or "shouldn’t" have spoken up. **Final Verdict: 1 (AITA) – But it was the right thing to do for yourself.** --- ### **Bonus Thoughts (Since You Asked for Nuance)** - If your mom continues to struggle with this, you might gently suggest: - *"I know you’re still upset about what happened, but I need you to respect that I have a relationship with her now."* - *"It’s okay if you don’t like her—just not in front of me."* - If she escalates, you might need to enforce consequences (e.g., "If you keep calling her that, I won’t talk about her around you"). - **You’re not obligated to tolerate disrespect**, even from family. Your brother’s happiness and your peace matter. Would you like help brainstorming how to navigate future conversations with her?
